title: Scheme-theoretic diagonal kernel of a triangular matrix group
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. All groups below are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] over $k$; subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness are as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] and [def-weil-connected-scheme]. For $n\geq1$, let $B_n\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_n$ be the group of invertible upper triangular matrices and $U_n\subseteq B_n$ its subgroup of matrices with every diagonal entry equal to $1$. Thus their $A$-points, for a commutative $k$-algebra $A$, are the matrices just described. The general linear group is [def-sc-general-linear-group]. Let $J\subseteq B_n$ be a closed subgroup. The diagonal map $\delta:J\to(\mathbf G_m)^n$, $g\mapsto(g_{11},\ldots,g_{nn})$, is a group-scheme homomorphism, with $\mathbf G_m$ as in [def-sc-gm-ga]. Put $V=\ker\delta=J\cap U_n$, the scheme-theoretic intersection. The subgroup $V$ is normal in $J$ and is unipotent in the scheme-theoretic sense of admitting a closed immersion into an upper unitriangular matrix group. The fppf sheaf quotient $D=J/V$ is represented by a group scheme, and $\delta$ induces a closed immersion $D\hookrightarrow(\mathbf G_m)^n$. If $k$ is algebraically closed, the quotient homomorphism $q:J\to D$ admits a group-scheme section $s:D\to J$; multiplication $(v,d)\mapsto v s(d)$ is an isomorphism of schemes $V\times_kD\simeq J$. In this case, if $J$ is smooth and connected, so are $V$ and $D$. In a smooth group this scheme-theoretic notion of unipotence is equivalent to every geometric point being a unipotent matrix in a faithful representation, that is, $(u-I)^N=0$ for some $N\geq1$. The fppf quotient means sheafification of $A\mapsto J(A)/V(A)$ for faithfully flat finitely presented coverings of commutative $k$-algebras.

source.place: Proposition 16.2(c)⇒(d), printed p.325; Theorem 16.26(a), printed pp.332–333 (splitting over an algebraically closed field); Note 16.10, printed p.326 (smoothness and connectedness via that splitting); Corollary 14.12, printed p.283 (geometric-point comparison for smooth groups).

proof.text: For upper triangular matrices over any commutative $k$-algebra $A$, $(gh)_{ii}=g_{ii}h_{ii}$ and $(g^{-1})_{ii}=g_{ii}^{-1}$. The diagonal coordinate functions therefore define a group-scheme homomorphism $\delta$. By [lem-sc-kernel-subgroup], its kernel is a closed subgroup, whose $A$-points are exactly the matrices of $J(A)$ with diagonal $1$. Thus it is the scheme-theoretic intersection $V=J\cap U_n$. For $j\in J(A)$ and $v\in V(A)$, $\delta(jvj^{-1})=1$, proving normality on every algebra. Affinely, imposing the equations of $J$ on $U_n$ gives a quotient of $k[x_{ij}:i<j]$, hence a closed immersion $V\hookrightarrow U_n$. This is the asserted scheme-theoretic unipotence.

source.place: Proposition 16.2(c)⇒(d), printed p.325; the kernel calculation is on all algebras, not only field-valued points.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization] to $\delta:J\to\mathbf G_m^n$. The kernel computed in step 1 is $V$, so this gives the represented fppf quotient $q:J\to D=J/V$ and a closed immersion $D\hookrightarrow\mathbf G_m^n$ inducing $\delta$. The groups are affine of finite type and hence separated, as required by the cited factorization. No assumption on $k$ beyond being a field is used here. For the rest of the proof assume $k$ algebraically closed. Apply the current statement of [lem-sfb-split-torus-subgroups-diagonalizable] with $F=k$, $r=n$ and $K=D$, using precisely the closed immersion just obtained. It gives an isomorphism of $k$-group schemes $D\simeq\operatorname{Spec}k[M]$ for a finitely generated abelian group $M$, with the group-algebra structure specified there. No smoothness, connectedness or finiteness of $D$ is needed for this conclusion.

source.place: Proposition 16.2(c)⇒(d), p.325; Theorem 5.39, p.108; Theorems 12.8 and 12.9(a),(c), pp.233--234.

proof.text: Take the filtration $U^{(r)}$ of [lem-sfb-unitriangular-coordinate-filtration], and put $V_r=J\cap U^{(r)}$. It is a series of subgroups normal in $J$, from $V_0=V$ to $V_m=1$. Restrict $p_r$ to $V_{r-1}$. Its scheme-theoretic kernel is $V_r$, so [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization] identifies $V_{r-1}/V_r$ with a closed subgroup of $\mathbf G_a$. The conjugation formula in the filtration node shows that this embedding is equivariant for the scalar character $t_{i_r}t_{j_r}^{-1}$ restricted to $D\subseteq\mathbf G_m^n$. Equality descends from $J$ to $D$ because $q$ is a sheaf quotient and the formula depends only on its diagonal image. Thus $V$ acts trivially on each factor. Equal successive $V_r$ can be omitted.

source.place: Example 6.49 and Theorem 16.21 proof, printed pp.136--137,330.

proof.text: Prove the following induction claim: an extension $1\to W\to E\to D\to1$ of affine finite-type groups, with $D$ diagonalizable and $W=W_0\supsetneq\cdots\supsetneq W_l=1$ normal in $E$, splits whenever each $W_{r-1}/W_r$ has a closed embedding in $\mathbf G_a$ equivariant for a scalar character of $D$. Induct on $l$. For $l=0$ the quotient map is an isomorphism. For $l>0$, put $N=W_{l-1}$. The quotient and correspondence assertions of [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] give $E/N\to D$ with kernel $W/N$ and its shorter inherited filtration. The induction hypothesis supplies a group section $s_N:D\to E/N$. In the pullback $P=E\times_{E/N,s_N}D$, the map $P\to D$ is an extension with kernel $N$. Indeed it is the base change of the quotient map $E\to E/N$, and the fibre and locally surjective sheaf descriptions are unchanged by pullback. The last factor embeds $N$ as a closed subgroup of $\mathbf G_a$ and gives exactly its scalar conjugation action through $D$. Apply [lem-sfb-additive-subgroup-diagonalizable-extension-splitting] to get a group section $t:D\to P$. Composing $t$ with $P\to E$ splits $E\to D$. This completes the induction. Step 3 verifies every filtration hypothesis for $E=J$, $W=V$, so we obtain $s:D\to J$.

source.place: Theorem 16.26 proof, printed pp.332--333, induction and pullback diagram (118); Theorem 15.34(d), p.319.

proof.text: The multiplication map $F:V\times_kD\to J$, $(v,d)\mapsto vs(d)$, has inverse $g\mapsto(g\,s(q(g))^{-1},q(g))$. The first component lies in $V$ since its image under $q$ is $q(g)q(g)^{-1}=1$. Both formulas are morphisms of schemes: they use multiplication, inverse, the section and the kernel's defining fibre product. Substituting either formula into the other gives the identity on every algebra, and the same identities hold for the morphisms. This proves the scheme isomorphism; no commutativity of $J$ or $V$ is asserted.

source.place: Theorem 16.26(a), pp.332--333; semidirect product interpretation, Section 2.34.

proof.text: Suppose also $J$ smooth and connected. Step 5 supplies scheme retractions $r_V:J\to V$ and $q:J\to D$, with sections $v\mapsto v$ and $s$. For $X=V$ or $D$, a map $T\to X$ from an affine first-order thickening $T\subset T'$ can first be composed with its section into $J$, lifted to $T'\to J$ by smoothness, and then composed with the retraction. Thus $X$ is formally smooth, directly by [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]. Both $X$ are affine finite type: for $V$ use step 1, and for $D$ its closed immersion in the torus. Their coordinate algebras are finite type by [lem-pc-affine-finite-type-algebra] and finitely presented by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-noetherian-finite-presentation], since a field is Noetherian (its only ideals are $0$ and $k$). Hence $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is locally of finite presentation and the cited definition makes it smooth. Each retraction is a continuous surjection. A separation of $X$ into nonempty clopen subsets would pull back to one of connected $J$, so both $V$ and $D$ are connected.

source.place: Note 16.10, printed p.326; explicit smooth-retraction lifting argument for the scheme product provided by 16.26(a).

proof.text: Finally let $G$ be a smooth affine finite-type group over an arbitrary field. If a faithful representation has all geometric points unipotent, [lem-sfb-geometric-unipotence-unitriangular-embedding] gives a closed immersion over the field into some upper unitriangular group. Conversely such an immersion is itself a faithful representation and every matrix $u=I+N$ in that group satisfies $N^n=0$: an entry of $N^n$ is a sum over strictly increasing chains of $n+1$ indices in a set of size $n$, and there are none. This proves the stated equivalence with the geometric-point formulation, with the smoothness hypothesis retained.

proof_origin.place: Proposition 16.2(c)⇒(d); Example 6.49; Theorems 16.21,16.26(a); Note 16.10; Corollary 14.12. Step 6 writes out the smooth-retraction argument.

lean.note: Closed subgroup of B_n is given by its closed GL_n inclusion with upper-triangular equations on every algebra. The diagonal map is specified by evaluating the Laurent coordinate of every G_m projection. The kernel square and the diagonal-one point criterion specify J intersect U_n scheme-theoretically; its closed GL_n inclusion with unitriangular equations gives the required closed U_n immersion. The second theorem is the final smooth geometric-unipotence comparison clause. Reuses the existing IsUnipotent and IsFppfGroupQuotient definitions, whose landed owner nodes are added to stmt_deps.
